highlights: Launched in March 1972 on an Atlas-Centaur rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Flew closest to Jupiter on December 3, 1973, about 130,000 km above the cloud tops.
On June 13, 1983, it crossed Neptune's orbit, the first spacecraft to pass beyond the planets.
NASA officially ended its science mission on March 31, 1997, but kept listening for its signal.
On February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 passed it to become the most distant human-made object.

highlights: Launched in April 1973 on an Atlas-Centaur rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Passed Jupiter on December 2, 1974, using its gravity as a slingshot toward Saturn.
Flew past Saturn on September 1, 1979, about 21,000 km above the clouds.
It made the first measurements of Saturn's magnetic field.
Earth heard its last signal in November 1995, when its power was too low to keep working.

links.title: Pioneer 11 in 3D (Eyes on the Solar System)
Pioneer data at the PDS Planetary Plasma Interactions Node

highlights: Launched on September 5, 1977, on a Titan IIIE-Centaur rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Flew past Jupiter on March 5, 1979, and spotted the first active volcanoes seen beyond Earth, on the moon Io.
Swung past Saturn on November 12, 1980, flying close to its hazy moon Titan.
Its cameras were switched off for good on February 14, 1990, right after its 'Family Portrait' of the planets.
On April 17, 2026, engineers turned off its low-energy charged particle instrument (LECP) to save power.
On November 18, 2026, it becomes the first human-made object one light-day (25.9 billion km) from Earth.

highlights: Launched on August 20, 1977, on a Titan IIIE-Centaur rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Visited Jupiter on July 9, 1979, and Saturn on August 25, 1981.
Reached Uranus on January 24, 1986, the first and only spacecraft to fly past it.
Flew about 5,000 km over Neptune's north pole on August 25, 1989, and saw its Great Dark Spot storm.
Crossed into interstellar space on November 5, 2018, six years after Voyager 1.
In 2024 engineers turned off its plasma science instrument to save power.

highlights: Launched on January 19, 2006, on an Atlas V rocket, the fastest spacecraft ever launched from Earth.
Got a speed boost from Jupiter's gravity on February 28, 2007, and photographed volcanoes erupting on Io.
On July 14, 2015, it passed about 12,500 km above Pluto's surface.
It took until late 2016 to send all of its Pluto pictures and data back to Earth.
On January 1, 2019, it flew about 3,500 km from Arrokoth, a snowman-shaped space rock.
In April 2020 it photographed nearby stars to show how their positions shift when seen from far away.

highlights: Launched on August 5, 2011, on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Swung past Earth on October 9, 2013, for a gravity boost toward Jupiter.
Arrived at Jupiter on July 4, 2016 (US time), the first solar-powered spacecraft to get there.
Flew close to Ganymede on June 7, 2021, and to Europa on September 29, 2022.
Passed about 1,500 km from the volcanic moon Io on December 30, 2023, and again on February 3, 2024.

Juno images at the PDS Imaging Node

highlights: Flew past Venus in February 1990 and Earth in December 1990 and December 1992 to gain speed.
On October 29, 1991, it took the first close-up pictures of an asteroid, Gaspra.
In July 1994 it had the only direct view of comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 crashing into Jupiter.
Went into orbit around Jupiter on December 7, 1995, the same day its probe dove in.
It made 35 orbits of Jupiter between 1995 and 2003.

links.title: Galileo in 3D (Eyes on the Solar System)
Galileo images at the PDS Imaging Node
Europa: Jupiter's Ocean World (NASA Space Place)

highlights: Launched on October 18, 1989, attached to the Galileo orbiter aboard Space Shuttle Atlantis.
Released from the orbiter on July 13, 1995, five months before reaching Jupiter.
Its heat shield slowed it from about 170,000 km/h to below the speed of sound in a few minutes.
It sank about 200 km into Jupiter's atmosphere before it stopped working.
It dropped into a rare dry, clear patch of Jupiter's clouds, which helps explain why it found so little water.

links.title: Galileo Probe in 3D (Eyes on the Solar System)
What's It Like Inside Jupiter? (NASA Space Place)

highlights: Launched on October 15, 1997, on a Titan IVB/Centaur rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Swung past Venus twice, Earth once and Jupiter (December 30, 2000) on the way to Saturn.
Fired its main engine to enter orbit around Saturn on July 1, 2004 (UTC).
Its passenger, Europe's Huygens probe, landed on Titan on January 14, 2005.
It made 294 orbits of Saturn and took more than 450,000 pictures.

links.title: Cassini in 3D (Eyes on the Solar System)
Cassini images at the PDS Imaging Node

highlights: Launched on August 3, 2004, on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Flew past Mercury three times (January 2008, October 2008, September 2009) before it could stay.
Entered orbit around Mercury on March 18, 2011 (UTC).
Found strange shallow pits called 'hollows' that may form as material escapes from Mercury's rocks.
Sent home more than 250,000 pictures before its fuel ran out.

links.title: MESSENGER in 3D (Eyes on the Solar System)
MESSENGER data at the PDS Geosciences Node

highlights: Space Shuttle Atlantis carried it to orbit on May 4, 1989; a rocket stage then sent it to Venus.
Went into orbit around Venus on August 10, 1990.
In 1993 it became the first planetary spacecraft to use 'aerobraking', skimming the air to shrink its orbit.
After radar mapping, it measured Venus's gravity to learn about the planet's insides.

links.title: Magellan in 3D (Eyes on the Solar System)
Magellan data at the PDS Geosciences Node

highlights: Launched on May 20, 1978, on an Atlas-Centaur rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Its radar mapped about 93% of Venus's surface, the first map of most of the planet.
It confirmed that Venus has almost no magnetic field of its own.
It found that Venus's upper air turns very cold on the night side.

links.title: Pioneer Venus data at the PDS Planetary Plasma Interactions Node

highlights: Launched on August 8, 1978, riding on the Multiprobe 'bus' on an Atlas-Centaur rocket.
Separated from the bus on November 16, 1978, about three weeks before reaching Venus.
It dropped its parachute about 47 km above the ground and fell freely the rest of the way.
The empty bus also dove into Venus that day, sending data until it burned up high in the air.

highlights: Launched on August 8, 1978, riding on the Multiprobe 'bus' with the Large Probe.
Released from the bus on November 20, 1978, and aimed at three far-apart spots on Venus.
All three entered Venus's atmosphere on December 9, 1978, within minutes of each other.
Each probe was a small ball about 0.8 meters across, with no parachute.

highlights: Launched on September 27, 2007, on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Swung past Mars in February 2009 for a gravity boost.
Orbited Vesta from July 16, 2011, to September 5, 2012.
Arrived at Ceres on March 6, 2015, and found a tall, lonely mountain, Ahuna Mons, likely an ice volcano.
Its ion engines changed its speed by about 11.5 km/s, a record for a spacecraft's own engines.

What Is an Asteroid? (NASA Space Place)

highlights: Launched on February 17, 1996, on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Flew past the dark asteroid Mathilde on June 27, 1997.
A failed engine burn in December 1998 made it miss Eros, so it looped around the Sun and tried again.
Renamed in March 2000 to honor planetary scientist Gene Shoemaker.

NEAR data at the PDS Small Bodies Node
What Is an Asteroid? (NASA Space Place)

highlights: Launched in March 2009 on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
In 2011 it confirmed Kepler-22b, its first planet found in a star's 'habitable zone'.
A second steering wheel broke in May 2013, ending its first mission.
In 2014 it found Kepler-186f, the first Earth-size planet in a habitable zone.
From 2014 it kept working as 'K2', using sunlight pressure to help hold steady.

links.title: Kepler in 3D (Eyes on the Solar System)
What Is an Exoplanet? (NASA Space Place)

highlights: Launched on August 25, 2003, on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
First called SIRTF, it was renamed in December 2003 after astronomer Lyman Spitzer.
In 2005 it was the first telescope to directly catch light from planets around other stars.
Its super-cold helium coolant ran out on May 15, 2009, but two cameras kept working in a 'warm mission'.

links.title: Spitzer in 3D (Eyes on the Solar System)
How's your infrared concentration? (NASA Space Place game)

highlights: Launched on January 12, 2005, on a Delta II rocket, attached to its flyby mothership.
Released from the mothership on July 3, 2005, about a day before impact.
It took pictures of the comet's surface until just seconds before it hit.
In 2011 Stardust saw the crater it left, about 150 meters wide.
Its mothership went on to fly past comet Hartley 2 on November 4, 2010.

What Is a Comet? (NASA Space Place)

highlights: Launched on February 7, 1999, on a Delta II rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Flew past asteroid Annefrank on November 2, 2002.
Passed about 240 km from comet Wild 2's icy core on January 2, 2004.
Its capsule landed in Utah on January 15, 2006, carrying comet dust and tiny grains from interstellar space.
Flew past comet Tempel 1 on February 14, 2011, as 'Stardust-NExT'.

highlights: Launched on November 24, 2021 (UTC), on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Vandenberg, California.
Its only camera, DRACO, sent a picture about every second until the crash.
Italy's tiny LICIACube satellite, released from DART on September 11, 2022, photographed the impact.
Hubble watched the crash make a tail of debris more than 10,000 km long.
Europe's Hera spacecraft launched on October 7, 2024, to study the crash site.

DART data at the PDS Small Bodies Node
What Is an Asteroid? (NASA Space Place)

highlights: Launched on September 8, 2016, on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
Arrived at asteroid Bennu on December 3, 2018, and mapped it for almost two years.
Left Bennu on May 10, 2021, carrying its sample home.
Its sample capsule landed in the Utah desert on September 24, 2023.
On September 23, 2025, it swung about 3,400 km past Earth on its way to Apophis.
Apophis will pass within 32,000 km of Earth in April 2029; the spacecraft arrives that June.
